base_rate.reference_class: Named Atlantic storm counts for the 1991-2020 climatological period
base_rate.basis: The 30-year mean is about 14 named storms per season, with a right-skewed distribution and a small number of hyperactive years well above 20.

status_quo: Sea-surface temperatures and the current ENSO outlook resemble the last several above-average seasons, so the count lands somewhat above the 30-year mean.

evidence_adjustments.claim: Pre-season sea-surface temperatures across the main development region are running about 1C above the 1991-2020 average.
The seasonal outlook gives roughly even odds of a weak La Nina developing, which historically favours more storm formation than a neutral or El Nino state.

load_bearing_facts.claim: The 30-year climatological mean is the anchor the adjustments move away from.

failure_modes: Saharan dust outbreaks early in the season can suppress formation well below what sea-surface temperatures alone would predict.
A late-developing La Nina would have less effect on the season than a La Nina already established by June.
rationale_summary: The climatological mean of about 14 storms is the starting point. Warmer than average sea-surface temperatures and favourable wind shear conditions this year both push the count upward, and a possible La Nina adds a further small push in the same direction. Uncertainty is wide because a single suppressing factor, such as a Saharan dust outbreak, has cut otherwise favourable seasons well below their preseason outlook before.
uncertainty_notes: Wind shear forecasts beyond two months carry limited skill and were not a strong independent input here.
